summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation carries criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve Sharia-administering states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Kogi does not administer Sharia, so the federal 14-year maximum is the operative ceiling there.

The statute's construction is settled. The Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014; entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, while registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

Partial constitutional relief exists. In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. The ruling does not extend to the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions. The Constitution contains no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation, and there are no national anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. The beaten body of the 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on a highway in the capital on 9 August 2024; she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life, and police opened an investigation. Police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. Six months after the killing no suspects had been charged, according to the Dial (February 2025). Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common in Nigeria, especially in the twelve Sharia states.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Official travel guidance reflects the risk. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states, and notes that the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Kogi's position as a non-Sharia state narrows the penalty range but does not remove it. The twelve Sharia-administering states impose harsher penalties than the federal 14-year maximum, with death penalties for lesbianism applied in Kano and Katsina according to the Wikipedia entry on LGBTQ rights in Nigeria; a visitor moving between states therefore faces a materially different exposure, and the FCDO advice flags death-penalty risk in Sharia states.

The 2022 constitutional ruling is itself unsettled territory for anyone assessing enforcement. It voided the provisions governing organisational activity while leaving the conduct and marriage provisions intact, and the sources record no comparable ruling striking those down. Whether the voided sections are honoured in practice by police on the ground is not established by the inventory.

The Bobrisky case is adjacent rather than determinative: it arose from currency abuse charges, not from identity or conduct, but it is the sources' only evidence of how the correctional system decides where to house a transgender prisoner, and the panel's finding that maximum-security placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act shows the placement question has been litigated administratively.

Enforcement in these sources is driven by extortion and opportunistic violence as much as by prosecution. The Lagos beating and bribe demand, the kito gangs using dating apps, and the reported commonality of mass detention suggest a risk profile that operates whether or not a case reaches court.
localsOnly:
Nigerian LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals may exist and organise on the strength of the 2022 ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act are unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide. That relief does not cover the conduct provisions or the marriage and civil-union prohibition, which remain in force.

The Constitution provides no specific protection on grounds of sexual orientation, and Nigeria has no national anti-discrimination statute covering LGBTQ people, so there is no general statutory complaint route for refusal of service, housing or employment on that basis.

Residents live with the reporting of the Abuja Area Mama case as an open matter: an investigation was opened in August 2024, an earlier stabbing in 2023 was reported, and as of February 2025 no suspect had been charged. The October 2024 panel's finding that maximum-security placement of Bobrisky breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act is the only adverse official finding against the correctional authorities recorded here.

Policing carries its own financial risk for residents: the Lagos incident involved a demand of 50,000 naira for a person stopped for looking gay, with release obtained by partial payment. Bribery allegations in the Bobrisky matter were dismissed by the investigative panel.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory records the proposals and the fear they generated, not their legislative status.

No Kogi-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory: there are no recorded arrests, prosecutions, state house of assembly legislation or state police directives from Kogi State itself. The Kogi assessment rests on the national statute, the Criminal Code, the Sharia comparison and nationally reported incidents.

The Human Rights Watch Nigeria country page (hrw.org/africa/nigeria) yielded no usable finding in this pass and supports none of the claims above.

Whether the 2022 ruling is observed in practice by police conducting stops and arrests is not sourced; the inventory documents the judgment and, separately, documented police conduct, but does not link them.
